claim: Gayed and Bilello (2016) show that using leverage when the broad U.S. equity market is above its Moving Average and deleveraging to Treasury bills when it is below produces better absolute and risk-adjusted returns than a comparable unleveraged buy-and-hold strategy or a constant-leverage strategy, and that this holds across various leverage amounts, Moving Average time periods, and multiple economic and financial market cycles.
limitations: SSRN working paper (2016 Charles H. Dow Award), not a peer-reviewed journal article; author-run backtest with author-chosen moving-average and leverage parameters; only the abstract was read locally (PDF not fetched), so the exact universe, sample period and cost assumptions are not yet independently verified; this is evidence for the general mechanism, not a claim about S3's specific 5-ETF menu, its 40 percent volatility target, or its dip boost.
quote: We establish that volatility is the enemy of leverage and that streaks in performance tend to be beneficial to using margin.

claim: Faber's updated (2013) tactical asset allocation study reports that a simple quantitative moving-average timing system continued to perform well in real time from 2008-2012, achieving equity-like returns with bond-like volatility and drawdowns across several asset classes, extending the original 2006 result.
limitations: SSRN working paper originally published in The Journal of Wealth Management (Spring 2007, a practitioner journal), updated 2013; uses a 10-month simple moving average on monthly closes across broad, unleveraged asset classes, not leveraged ETFs, not S3's specific menu, and not a 200-session daily gate; only the abstract was read locally (PDF not fetched).
quote: Overall, we find that the models have performed well in real-time, achieving equity like returns with bond like volatility and drawdowns.

claim: An independent real-money, publicly-tracked implementation of the Gayed and Bilello Leverage-for-the-Long-Run rule (2x S&P 500 ETF SSO while the S&P 500 closes above its 200-day moving average, else BIL) has been running live since March 2024 with monthly Reddit updates; as of the September 2026 update it remains fully invested in SSO because the S&P 500 is still above its 200-day moving average, and the author states the portfolio has been followed strictly with no additional contributions.
limitations: Single anonymous retail author's self-reported real-money account on r/LETFs, not independently audited; only the current allocation state and cumulative narrative are given in the posts read so far -- no verified since-inception return table has been located locally yet (also noted in this repo's own dir:letf_published_rules_live_tracked); demonstrates only that the gate is currently on (a single observed state), not that it avoids whipsaw or adds value net of costs; the instrument (SSO, 2x S&P 500) differs from S3's menu (TQQQ/SOXL/UPRO/USD/TECL) and from all four gate assets tested here.
quote: The underlying S&P 500 index (7,686) remains above its 200-day moving average (7,122). The full balance will remain invested in SSO until the S&P 500 closes below its 200-day MA.
